Exact waves on a single light ray

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and figure: CC0.

A wave can be nonzero throughout spacetime while all its singularities travel along one line. We construct an explicit solution of the homogeneous wave equation in three spatial dimensions. Its ordinary and analytic wavefront sets contain exactly one positive covector ray above every point of that line. Taking its real part gives both signs. A positive-frequency plane-wave representation explains how smooth Gaussian packets produce this singular limit.

The boundary theorem used below is Theorem 5 of Imaginary displacements and microhyperbolic cones. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 6 and 5, supplies the comparison with ordinary wavefront and the analytic singular-support projection. The ordinary projection and finite-sum argument are proved in Lemma 1 of A whole characteristic line with smooth forcing. Theorem 4 of Analytic pullback and cotangent directions supplies the analytic coordinate law. For the integral representation we use Theorem 3.1 of Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, with the exact Fourier convention in Schwartz Fourier foundations, F1–F5. The integration foundations, Sections 15–16, and polar integration, A4–A5, justify the absolute integral estimates.

Proposition 4 (real fields have both signs). Each of and solves the same homogeneous equation. For both fields, both wavefront sets equal the set in (12) with .

Proof. Complex conjugation commutes with the wave operator, whose coefficients are real. For a compact distribution and a real cutoff,

Thus conjugation reverses ordinary wavefront directions. It reverses analytic directions as well: conjugate the bounded compact distributions in the defining analytic regularity sequence and use (13). Boundedness and every Fourier estimate are preserved, with the cone reflected. Apply conjugation twice to obtain equality.

The wavefront of a sum is contained in the union. If either real or imaginary part were regular there, expressing as a linear combination of that part and would contradict (12). At a negative ray interchange the roles. The two finite-sum inclusions exclude every other direction. This proves both equalities.

Exercise 7 (intermediate: which linear combinations retain a sign?). For complex constants , determine both wavefront sets of .

Solution. If , both are empty. If precisely one coefficient is nonzero, multiplication by that nonzero constant preserves the wavefront and selects its corresponding sign. If both are nonzero, the sets are the union of the positive and negative rays in Proposition 4. At a positive ray the conjugate term is regular, so regularity of the combination would imply regularity of after subtraction and division by . The negative-ray argument uses . The sum inclusion gives the reverse bound. This argument applies to ordinary and analytic regularity alike.

Exercise 8 (advanced: finitely many exact singular light rays). Prescribe finitely many distinct oriented affine light lines , with , and a nonzero complex coefficient for each. Construct a homogeneous wave solution whose ordinary and analytic wavefronts are exactly the union of their positive covector rays.

Solution. Use (10) on each line, with any , and take the finite linear combination. Each summand solves the homogeneous equation globally, so their sum does too. Two distinct lines with the same are parallel and disjoint. If two of the lines meet but have different , their selected covectors are not positive multiples: equality of the time components would force the scaling factor to be one and then force the directions to agree. Hence the selected wavefront sets of the distinct summands are disjoint even over an intersection point. At every prescribed covector all the other summands are microlocally regular. Subtracting those summands forces that covector to remain, while the finite-sum inclusion excludes all others.
